Motoring groups say fuel prices in the UK aren't falling fast enough after the drop in oil prices over recent weeks.

And in Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis make further advances along the Red Sea coast and push towards the government capital of Aden.

description:
Can Nvidia survive without the man who built it?

This week on BBC AI Decoded, we tackle the biggest story in artificial intelligence and Silicon Valley: the shock departure of Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang.

After 33 years at the helm, Huang has stepped down amid explosive allegations involving two extra-marital affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of links to Chinese espionage. The controversy has triggered political fallout in Washington, sparked questions about how advanced AI chips reached China, and intensified scrutiny of the company at the centre of the global AI boom.

And this week we have an exclusive interview with Paul Mozur, one of the New York Times journalists who helped break the story that sent shockwaves through the tech industry.

description:
Alan Milburn's long awaited report into young people not in education, employment, or training - "Neet" - has been published.

Nearly one million young people in the UK are not earning or learning. In his report, Milburn sets out an extensive set of reforms to try and reach a target he calls Neet Zero… or reducing the number of young Neets down from 15% to 5% by 2036.

Adam and Chris Mason are joined by education and family editor, Branwen Jeffreys, to unpack the 267-page report and assess how feasible its recommendations are.

BBC Panorama can reveal the Metropolitan Police missed opportunities to stop predatory detective, Warren Arter, from sexually exploiting vulnerable victims of crime, whose cases he investigated.
 
Warren Arter used his position to target the very women it was his job to protect, including his future wife, Rebekah, whose sexual abuse he filmed and distributed before she died in mysterious circumstances in Barbados two years ago.
 
A former detective inspector who began an investigation into Arter in 2016 claims senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiry despite him finding multiple potential victims.
 
Arter's abuse spanned almost 20 years until his death on remand in HMP Wandsworth in 2024. The Met has not reviewed all the cases he was involved with.
 
The Met told the BBC it was deeply sorry - and encouraged anyone who believes they were abused by him to come forward.

author: BBC News
description:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenzhen, China, this week, for their first-ever trilateral summit. President Trump has said the agenda will include denuclearisation, the war with Iran, and the war in Ukraine. So what could emerge from this meeting? Some analysts are hopeful that China could exert some influence on Tehran, and act as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he's worried that the three leaders could try to reshape the international order as they fit, without consulting smaller countries. 

Trump, Putin and Xi are also expected to talk about the economy and AI, particularly after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO of Nvidia, following allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. This video brings together our China specialist, our correspondent in Washington, and our Russia and Ukraine analyst.

author: BBC News
description:
For decades, computer scientists have been trying to figure out whether computers can think. But with the advent of highly sophisticated chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT … might we finally have our answer? 

This week we’re introducing The Global Backstory, the new strand of our show that explores the history behind the news today. We constantly hear stories about artificial intelligence, but most of them are about where AI is going; in this five-episode series we’re looking at where it came from.

Beginning with computer scientist Alan Turing’s famous Turing test in 1950, the quest to verify the existence of machine intelligence has taken on many forms – from the rudimentary chatbots of the 1960s, to the 1997 defeat of a chess grand master by a computer, to IBM Watson’s stint on Jeopardy in the 2010s.

But large language models have rendered old methods of measuring machine intelligence obsolete. So how smart is AI, anyway? And will it ever be smarter than us? Tristan Redman and Asma
title: Will AI ever be smarter than us? | BBC News

description:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
 
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.
 
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the attack, though he is yet to comment.
 
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

description:
A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand says she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" he was able to claim innocence from prison, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.
 
Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
 
Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and Brand denies her claims.
 
Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.

A "complete system reset" is needed to get hundreds of thousands of young people into jobs or training, according to a former Labour minister.
 
The UK government has tasked Alan Milburn to provide his proposals on how to help young people who are not in work or education, or training (Neet), with the report due to be published on Tuesday.
 
Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are Neet, a rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.

author: BBC News
description:
There are nearly one million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are Neet.

That is a young person who is not in education, employment, or training - and the number is rising.  

It costs the the taxpayer billions and has seen hundreds of thousands of young people struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

We spoke to four of those young people to find out what it’s really like to be Neet for the day.

Former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn was commissioned by the UK government to make recommendations on how to bring the Neet figures down. That year-long report is published on Tuesday.

This will include recommendations to overhaul of the benefit system for under-25s and invest billions in workplace opportunities.
